title: Two more poems
author: Shénbǐ
description: 悯农 (why you shouldn't waste rice) and 相思 (red beans for a friend you miss). Like the game's own poems, they fill in by themselves as you learn their words.

poems.title: 悯农
poems.story: Almost every Chinese child knows this poem: parents say its last line at dinner when rice is left in the bowl. Lǐ Shēn watched farmers working in the summer heat and wrote it so that people eating in comfort would remember where their food comes from.

lines.en: Hoeing the grain under the noon sun,
lines.explain: A farmer weeds his rice field at noon, the hottest hour of the day.

lines.en: his sweat drips onto the soil beneath the grain.
lines.explain: The work is so hard that his sweat falls drop by drop onto the earth.

lines.en: Who knows that the food in our bowls —
lines.explain: The poet turns to us, the people eating: do we ever think about it?

lines.en: every single grain comes from hard work?
lines.explain: Each grain of rice cost someone sweat, so don't waste food. 粒粒 doubled means 'every one'.

poems.title: 相思
poems.story: Red beans, the shiny red seeds of a tree from the warm south of China, were called 'missing-you seeds' (相思子). People gave them to friends far away. Wáng Wéi, a poet and painter, sent this little poem to a friend he missed.

lines.en: Red beans grow in the south;
lines.explain: 红豆 are the 'missing-you seeds'; 南国 is the warm south of China.

lines.en: when spring comes, how many new branches sprout?
lines.explain: The poet wonders about the tree far away, as he wonders about his friend.

lines.en: I hope you pick a lot of them,
lines.explain: 君 is a polite old word for 'you'. He asks his friend to gather the seeds.

lines.en: for nothing makes us miss each other more.
lines.explain: Every red bean you hold will remind you of your friend: that's the gift.
